questions.correct_answer: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
questions.explanation: RAG is basically AI's long-term memory — it actually looks stuff up (like your company docs) instead of just relying on training data. From the anatomy slide: brain = LLM, long-term memory = RAG.
questions.question: Which AI thing is basically your long-term memory's twin?

choices: Confident false memories or vivid dreams
questions.correct_answer: Confident false memories or vivid dreams
questions.explanation: Hallucinations are basically AI's dream state — vivid, confident, sometimes 100% made up. It's not lying on purpose, it just doesn't know what it doesn't know. That's exactly why P.R.O.M.P.T. exists — guardrails around what AI can and can't invent.
questions.question: AI hallucinations are basically the human version of what?

questions.correct_answer: 90–120 days
questions.explanation: Old-school enterprise software takes 90-120 days just to get a baseline working. OrchestrAI compresses that to 7 days. That's a 17x speedup — not from working harder, just cutting work that never needed to exist.
questions.question: How long does it usually take to get a baseline working, the old-school way?

questions.correct_answer: QA (Quality Assurance)
questions.explanation: OrchestrAI delivers an 80% baseline to the client's QA in 7 days. Last 20% gets built together during UAT. Go-live only happens once the client's actually confident — not a second before. Fast, but never reckless.
questions.question: OrchestrAI ships to the client's ___ environment in 7 days — not straight to production.

choices: Solo violinist — total control of one instrument
Orchestra conductor — commands eighty musicians without touching one
Music critic — judges performance from the audience
Studio engineer — mixes after the recording is done
questions.correct_answer: Orchestra conductor — commands eighty musicians without touching one
questions.explanation: The conductor analogy is the main idea of this whole program. A soloist's hands are literally on the instrument. A conductor's hands touch nothing — but commands way more, through a score written with total precision beforehand. That's the shift: stop playing the instrument, start writing the score.
questions.question: Which analogy best describes what an OrchestrAI Lead actually does?

choices: In the QA cycle, by dedicated testers
Upstream, in the prompt and brief
questions.correct_answer: Upstream, in the prompt and brief
questions.explanation: Don't filter the river, clean the source. Old-world QA catches defects after they've already flowed through everything. OrchestrAI builds quality in upstream, in the brief itself. Every bug caught in QA traces back to a vague brief. Every compliance miss in UAT traces back to a missing Marker.
questions.question: Where does quality actually get built in, in the OrchestrAI model?

choices: Model — which AI model to use
questions.correct_answer: Marker — hard constraints and guardrails
questions.explanation: Marker = the guardrails. Hard, non-negotiable rules — budget, compliance, what's off-limits, approved tools only. Without Markers, AI will confidently break your business rules without even knowing it's doing it. Honestly the most important letter for keeping hallucinations from causing real damage.
questions.question: What's the 'M' in P.R.O.M.P.T. actually stand for?

choices: AI gives a generic, non-expert response that needs heavy rework
AI asks you a clarifying question
AI defaults to the most recent role from your last session
questions.correct_answer: AI gives a generic, non-expert response that needs heavy rework
questions.explanation: Without Role, AI defaults to generic 'helpful assistant' mode — broad, surface-level, not specialized at all. Saying 'act as a senior payments architect with 10 years at FIS' completely changes the depth, vocabulary, everything. Same model, same prompt, just swap Role — night and day difference.
questions.question: If you skip 'Role' in your P.R.O.M.P.T., what usually happens?

questions.correct_answer: Output and Pattern
questions.explanation: Output sets the format — markdown table, JSON, React component, whatever. Pattern sets the internal structure — day-by-day, header-form-footer, etc. Together, they make the output ready to actually use, not ready to rewrite. Purpose and Role are the what and who. Marker and Tone are the rules and the vibe.
questions.question: Which two parts of P.R.O.M.P.T. control the actual shape AI hands back to you?

choices: End of the first sprint, around day 10
Same day as intent capture — around 11:30 AM
questions.correct_answer: Same day as intent capture — around 11:30 AM
questions.explanation: 9 AM intent capture, 10:30 first generation cycle, 11:30 you're showing a live screen to the business owner. That's the Mission Control rhythm — quick decision bursts, long stretches of supervising, real working software by mid-morning, day one. Not a mockup. The actual thing.
questions.question: In a typical OrchestrAI day, when does the business owner actually see a real working screen?

comparison_report.closing_line: Compare your six fields to the AI version above. Wherever you were thin, that's your growth edge for Lab 2.

common_gaps.insight: This is the one people skip most. 'Budget per person,' 'no alcohol-based activities,' 'rain backup' — these aren't details, they're the difference between a usable plan and a plan you have to rewrite. If your Marker section was thin, that's completely normal on a first attempt — and exactly why this lab exists.
Notice how 'an experienced corporate event planner' produces a different quality of answer than no role at all. AI without a Role defaults to generic — same as we covered in slide 14.

Without a Pattern, AI might give you a paragraph instead of a scannable schedule. Specifying 'morning, afternoon, evening blocks' turns a wall of text into something you could actually forward to your manager.

comparison_report.intro: Here's the thing — there's no single 'correct' answer in this lab. The goal is to see what a fully-loaded P.R.O.M.P.T. looks like, and notice which of the six elements you instinctively filled in strong, and which ones you might have skipped.

common_gaps.insight: 'Under 60 seconds to fill out' and 'no collecting personal info beyond the order record' look like small details, but they're actually the constraints that prevent a bloated, privacy-risky form from getting built. This is exactly the upstream-quality idea from slide 12 — these Markers prevent problems before they exist.

Did you just say 'a feedback form'? Or did you specify what comes back — a working component, documentation, both? Vague Output means you might get a paragraph describing a form instead of an actual buildable spec.

This one's easy to forget on a 'technical' request — but the actual words a customer sees on that form matter. 'Warm and appreciative' versus no tone guidance at all is the difference between a form that feels human and one that feels like a compliance checkbox.

formal.narration: The OrchestrAI governance framework is built on six core principles. First: AI as Primary Builder. The AI engine generates all code artifacts; manual intervention breaks version control. Second: Human as Orchestrator. The Lead defines parameters and controls quality. Third: Plain-English Driven. Requirements are structured in precise natural language. Fourth: Continuous Delivery. Delivery is continuous rather than boxed into sprints. Fifth: Instant Iteration. Code correction happens in real-time. And sixth: Quality by Design. Security and validation are defined in the intent statement.

flaws.explanation: No Validation Rules. What makes an expense valid? Required fields? Amount limits? Duplicate detection? Without numbered rules, AI will guess — and guess wrong.
No Security Constraints. Who enforces that a Manager can only see their team's expenses? Client-side only? Server-side? Both? Without this, data leaks.
No Edge Cases. What if a Manager IS the submitter? What about expenses submitted after the period closes? What if the VP is on leave? These become production bugs.

formal.narration: We must avoid five common intent anti-patterns. First: the Vague Outcome, which lacks scope and specifications. Second: the Mega-Prompt, which attempts to generate large systems in a single pass, degrading output quality. Third: the Assumption Prompt, which fails to specify dependencies. Fourth: the Trust-and-Skip, which accepts code without verification. Fifth: the Manual Patch, which updates code directly, creating code drift.

after.output: 'Build a timesheet entry screen for Team Members (role: TEAM_MEMBER). 7-day grid, Mon-Sun, rows for project/task pairs. 10 validation rules: (1) at least one complete row, (2) project mandatory, (3) task mandatory, (4) no duplicate project+task, (5) daily hours 0-24, (6) task not expired, (7-8) no hours outside task date range, (9) daily total <=24h, (10) weekly total >=40h. flaws.explanation: No Validation Rules. What makes an expense valid? Required fields? Amount limits? Duplicate detection? Without numbered rules, AI will guess — and guess wrong.
No Security Constraints. Who enforces that a Manager can only see their team's expenses? Client-side only? Server-side? Both? Without this, data leaks.
No Edge Cases. What if a Manager IS the submitter? What about expenses submitted after the period closes? What if the VP is on leave? These become production bugs.

analogy.text: 'Close enough' is the most expensive phrase in software. A vague intent that seems 80% right generates code that's 80% right — and that last 20% costs more to fix than writing the whole intent properly would have.

list.desc: Accepting output without checking. AI is statistically good but not always correct. Fix: validate every output. No exceptions.

genz.narration: Here are the five ways intent goes wrong. Avoid these like the plague. First: the Vague Outcome — saying 'build a dashboard' with no detail. Second: the Mega-Prompt — trying to generate the whole app in one go. Third: the Assumption Prompt — assuming AI knows how you do auth. Fourth: the Trust-and-Skip — accepting code without testing. Fifth: the Manual Patch — fixing code yourself instead of correcting the prompt. Remember: close enough is the most expensive phrase in software.

common_gaps.insight: Always test with cross-tenant context. Trying to fetch data using another user's ID is the absolute best way to check if your server-side checks actually hold up.

narration_script.text: Fifth, deployment guardrails. Controlled CI/CD pipelines. Approval checkpoints. Security validation prior to promotion. The pipeline itself functions as a guardrail.

bullets: OUTCOME — authenticated users access protected routes via valid JWT; unauthenticated requests receive 401.
ACTOR — three roles: Admin, Manager, Reporter — each with distinct menu visibility.
VALIDATION — email format, password minimum eight characters with mixed case, account lockout after five failed attempts.
SECURITY — bcrypt hashing at cost 12, JWT expiry 24 hours, refresh token rotation, server-side guards on every protected route.
STACK — NestJS @nestjs/jwt with Passport, Prisma User model, React Context for client-side authentication state.
ACCEPTANCE — successful login returns 200 with token; invalid credentials return 401; expired tokens trigger redirect to /login.
EDGE CASES — empty fields, malformed email, brute force attempts, token expiry during active session.
DATA MODEL — User entity: id, email UNIQUE, passwordHash, role ENUM, createdAt, lastLoginAt.

bullets: OUTCOME: Users with email + password can log in; protected routes require a valid JWT.
ACTOR: Admin, Manager, Reporter — three roles with different menu access.
VALIDATION: Email format, password ≥ 8 chars with mixed case, account-locked after 5 failed attempts.
SECURITY: Bcrypt hash (cost 12), JWT with 24h expiry, refresh tokens, server-side guards on EVERY protected route.
STACK: NestJS @nestjs/jwt + Passport, Prisma User model, React Context for auth state.
ACCEPTANCE: Valid login → 200 + token, invalid → 401, token expired → 401 with redirect to /login.
EDGE CASES: Empty fields, malformed email, brute force, expired token mid-action.
DATA MODEL: User { id, email UNIQUE, passwordHash, role ENUM, createdAt, lastLoginAt }.

bullets: Bad re-prompt: 'fix performance' — vague, AI guesses. Don't do this.
Good re-prompt: 'In dashboard.service.ts, getDashboardMetrics() is making 4 separate Prisma calls. Combine into 1 query using groupBy + raw aggregations.'
AI returns: a single Prisma $queryRaw with COUNT/SUM groupings, drops query count from 4 → 1.
Add: 'Also add @@index([assigneeId, status]) and @@index([dueDate]) to schema.prisma.' Two re-prompts. Done.
Total dashboard time including re-prompts: ~90 minutes. From zero to shipped + indexed.

genz.title: The 3 Admin Surfaces — Why RBAC Always Needs Humans

bullets: Unlike Workflow (ONE long prompt), admin surfaces work best as 3 focused prompts — one per surface.
Why? Each surface has different RBAC, different validation, different list/detail UX. Splitting keeps each tight.
EVERY admin prompt must include: 'RBAC: which role can do what (matrix below). Server enforces on every endpoint. UI hides actions a role cannot perform.'
Example RBAC clause for Project Setup: 'Admin: full CRUD. Manager: full CRUD on their accessible projects. Reporter: read-only on their accessible projects. Server-side check at controller layer.'
Commit after EACH surface validates. 3 surfaces = 3 commits = 3 push events on Day 6.

genz.narration: Five common AI report bugs. Excel column types — everything stored as text. PDF page breaks — rows split mid-cell. Tenant leakage — Manager sees all projects. narration_script.speaker: Sara
narration_script.text: Five common AI report bugs. Each one — caught by manual spot-check before QA finds them.

narration_script.speaker: Arjun
narration_script.text: One — Excel column types. AI ships everything as text by default. Re-prompt — date columns formatted as dates, numbers as numbers, currency with currency formatting.

narration_script.speaker: Sara
narration_script.text: Two — PDF page breaks. Rows split across pages mid-cell. Repeat header on each page. No orphan rows. Three — tenant leakage. Manager sees all projects globally. Re-prompt the where-clause scoping.

narration_script.speaker: Arjun
narration_script.text: Four — internal IDs exposed. UUIDs in client-facing columns. Never. Use reporter names, assignee names, project names.

narration_script.speaker: Sara
narration_script.text: Five — performance. Thirty seconds for ten thousand rows. Prisma raw SQL plus indexes plus a LIMIT cap with a note in the subtitle. AI is great at structure. Weak at finish. You finish.

table.orch: ✅ Date columns formatted as dates, numbers as numbers, currency formatted
